title: What is a Jenkins Scripted vs Declarative pipeline, and what is Groovy's role in a `Jenkinsfile`?
shortTitle: Jenkins Scripted vs Declarative Pipeline and Groovy's Role in a Jenkinsfile

s1_definition.profdef: A `Jenkinsfile` defines a pipeline as code and can be written in two styles. A Declarative pipeline uses a structured, opinionated syntax wrapped in a top-level `pipeline { }` block with predefined sections like `agent`, `stages`, `steps`, `environment`, `post`, and built-in constructs for conditions and approvals; it is easier to read and validate. A Scripted pipeline is written as a Groovy program inside a `node { }` block with full imperative control such as loops, variables, functions, and try/catch; it is more flexible but more error-prone. Both are executed by the Jenkins Groovy engine, so Groovy is the underlying language in both cases: Declarative is a Groovy-based domain-specific language with guardrails, while Scripted is closer to raw Groovy.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of two ways to write the National Bank of India's cheque-processing procedure. The Declarative way is a standard printed form with fixed boxes: "Branch:", "Steps:", "Approval:", "On failure:". Anyone can fill it in correctly and a supervisor can glance at it and immediately see if a box is missing. The Scripted way is a blank notebook where you write the whole procedure freehand in full sentences, with if-this-then-that logic and loops; it can express anything, but it is easier to make a mistake and harder for a supervisor to check. Both notebooks and forms are ultimately read by the same clerk (the Groovy engine) who carries out the instructions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Declarative is a structured Groovy DSL with guardrails for readability, Scripted is free-form Groovy for maximum flexibility, and Groovy is the engine running both.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `Jenkinsfile` defines a pipeline as code and can be written in two styles. A Declarative pipeline uses a structured, opinionated syntax wrapped in a top-level `pipeline { }` block with predefined sections like `agent`, `stages`, `steps`, `environment`, `post`, and built-in constructs for conditions and approvals; it is easier to read and validate. A Scripted pipeline is written as a Groovy program inside a `node { }` block with full imperative control such as loops, variables, functions, and try/catch; it is more flexible but more error-prone. Both are executed by the Jenkins Groovy engine, so Groovy is the underlying language in both cases: Declarative is a Groovy-based domain-specific language with guardrails, while Scripted is closer to raw Groovy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of two ways to write the National Bank of India's cheque-processing procedure. The Declarative way is a standard printed form with fixed boxes: "Branch:", "Steps:", "Approval:", "On failure:". Anyone can fill it in correctly and a supervisor can glance at it and immediately see if a box is missing. The Scripted way is a blank notebook where you write the whole procedure freehand in full sentences, with if-this-then-that logic and loops; it can express anything, but it is easier to make a mistake and harder for a supervisor to check. Both notebooks and forms are ultimately read by the same clerk (the Groovy engine) who carries out the instructions.

**One line to remember:** Declarative is a structured Groovy DSL with guardrails for readability, Scripted is free-form Groovy for maximum flexibility, and Groovy is the engine running both.

sections.s2_technical:
A Declarative pipeline always starts with `pipeline { }` at the top level. Inside it you declare an `agent` (where it runs), an `environment` block for variables, a `stages` block containing named `stage` blocks, and each stage has a `steps` block with the actual commands. For example a stage looks like `stage('Build') { steps { sh 'mvn clean package' } }`. Declarative gives you built-in sections such as `post { always { } success { } failure { } }` for cleanup and notifications, `when { branch 'main' }` for conditional execution, `input` for approvals, and `options` for things like timeouts. Jenkins validates the structure up front, so a malformed Declarative pipeline is rejected before it runs.

A Scripted pipeline starts with `node { }` and is essentially a Groovy script. You write imperative code directly: assign variables, use `if` and `for`, define functions, and call steps like `stage('Build') { sh 'mvn clean package' }`. Because it is a real program you can do things like loop over a list of microservices and build each, or compute a deployment target from arbitrary logic. The cost is that there are fewer guardrails; a typo or a logic bug surfaces at runtime, and the structure is harder for a reviewer to scan.

Groovy is central to both. Jenkins pipelines run on a Groovy interpreter (specifically a sandboxed, continuation-passing variant called CPS so pipelines can survive a controller restart). In a Declarative pipeline, Groovy still appears inside a `script { }` block when you need real logic, for example `script { def tag = sh(returnStdout: true, script: 'git rev-parse HEAD').trim() }`. In a Scripted pipeline the whole file is Groovy. Understanding Groovy matters because you use its string interpolation, collections, closures, and the `sh`, `echo`, and `error` steps that Jenkins exposes.

Shared Libraries bring the two worlds together. Reusable logic is written as Groovy in a versioned repository and called from either style, for example `bankDeploy(service: 'transfer-service', env: 'qa')`. This keeps the per-service `Jenkinsfile` tiny while the complex Groovy lives in one audited place.

A senior nuance is when to choose each. The strong default in a regulated banking environment is Declarative, because its structure is easy to read, review, and validate, and the standard sections cover almost everything. You drop into a `script { }` block or a Shared Library for the rare bits of real logic. Pure Scripted is reserved for genuinely dynamic needs, such as generating stages at runtime for an unknown number of services, and even then the logic is usually pushed into a Shared Library so the pipeline file stays clean. Another nuance is the CPS sandbox: not all Groovy is allowed, certain methods are blocked for security, and heavy in-pipeline Groovy computation is discouraged because it runs on the controller, not the agent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh wrote the first pipeline as a free-form Scripted file with lots of if-else logic to decide which environment to deploy to. It worked, but when Priya tried to review it before an audit she could not quickly tell what the stages were or what happened on failure, because it was buried in Groovy logic. This is exactly the problem the Declarative style solves. Declarative forces a clear structure with named stages and a post block, so a reviewer sees the shape of the pipeline instantly.

Problem 2 — The team had twelve microservices and each copy-pasted the same forty lines of deploy logic. When they needed to add a vulnerability scan, they had to edit twelve files and missed two. This is exactly the problem Groovy Shared Libraries solve. The deploy logic lives once as Groovy in a versioned library, and each service calls a single step, so a change is made in one audited place.

Problem 3 — Occasionally the team genuinely needed dynamic behaviour, such as building a variable list of services discovered at runtime. Pure Declarative could not express that cleanly. This is exactly where a Groovy `script { }` block or Scripted logic earns its place, kept small and ideally inside the library.

To make this concrete without a Jenkins server we will write a small Java simulation that contrasts the two styles. We will model a `DeclarativePipeline` as a fixed, ordered structure of named stages with a post-action, and a `ScriptedPipeline` as a class that builds its stages with arbitrary imperative logic (a loop over services). We will also model a `SharedLibrary` step `bankDeploy` that both styles call, proving reuse. We will run a Declarative pipeline for the transfer service and a Scripted pipeline that dynamically builds a deploy stage per service, so you can see the structured versus free-form difference side by side.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jenkins-pipeline-styles-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/pipeline/
│   │   │   ├── PipelineStylesDemo.java        (main runnable demo)
│   │   │   ├── Stage.java                     (a named stage)
│   │   │   ├── SharedLibrary.java             (reusable bankDeploy step)
│   │   │   ├── DeclarativePipeline.java       (fixed structure + post)
│   │   │   └── ScriptedPipeline.java          (imperative stage building)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── logging.properties
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/pipeline/
│           └── PipelineStylesTest.java
├── Jenkinsfile.declarative                    (real declarative example)
└── Jenkinsfile.scripted                       (real scripted example)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -cp target/classes com.bank.pipeline.PipelineStylesDemo

# Real usage: place Jenkinsfile.declarative or Jenkinsfile.scripted in the repo
# and point a Jenkins pipeline job at it. Validate declarative syntax with:
# curl -X POST -F "jenkinsfile=<Jenkinsfile.declarative" https://jenkins.bank.local/pipeline-model-converter/validate
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Jenkinsfile
    │
    ├─ DECLARATIVE STYLE               ├─ SCRIPTED STYLE
    │   pipeline {                     │   node {
    │     agent { label 'k8s' }        │     def services = [...]
    │     stages {                     │     for (svc in services) {
    │       Build  → mvn package       │       stage("Deploy ${svc}")
    │       Test   → mvn test          │         → bankDeploy(svc, dev)
    │       DeployQA → bankDeploy()    │     }
    │     }                            │   }
    │     post { always { ... } }      │
    ▼                                  ▼
  Groovy CPS engine (same executor for both)
    │                                  │
    └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                   ▼
         SharedLibrary.bankDeploy(service, env)   ← reused by BOTH styles
                   │
                   ▼
           kubectl rollout command
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Pipeline Style Classes ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Builder Pattern: DeclarativePipeline.stage().post().run()      │
  │     WHY: readable, chained construction of a fixed structure     │
  │  Template/Reuse: SharedLibrary.bankDeploy() one step, many uses │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Stage holds one step; SharedLibrary builds deploy steps     │
  │  O: new deploy target? call bankDeploy with new env, no rewrite │
  │  D: both pipelines depend on SharedLibrary, not inline commands │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌─────────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │   DeclarativePipeline   │     │    ScriptedPipeline     │
  │ - agentLabel            │     │                         │
  │ - stages: List<Stage>   │     │ + run(services, env)    │
  │ - postAlways: String    │     │   (imperative loop)     │
  │ + stage(Stage): this    │     └───────────┬─────────────┘
  │ + post(String): this    │                 │ both call
  │ + run(): void           │                 ▼
  └───────────┬─────────────┘     ┌─────────────────────────┐
              │ contains           │     SharedLibrary       │
              ▼                    │ + bankDeploy(svc,env):  │
  ┌─────────────────────────┐     │     Stage (static)      │
  │        Stage            │◀────┘                         │
  │ - name, action          │     └─────────────────────────┘
  └─────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Pipeline Authoring Choice ──────────────

  [NEED PIPELINE] → fixed stages, needs review? ─yes─→ [DECLARATIVE]
        │ no (dynamic stage count at runtime)
        ▼
  [SCRIPTED] → heavy logic? ─yes─→ push into [SHARED LIBRARY]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. new DeclarativePipeline("k8s")
  2.   .stage(Build).stage(Test)
  3.   .stage(SharedLibrary.bankDeploy("transfer-service","qa"))
  4.   .post(...).run()                     → prints fixed structure
  5. new ScriptedPipeline().run([svc1,svc2,svc3],"dev")
  6.   → for each svc: SharedLibrary.bankDeploy(svc,"dev")
  7.   → prints one dynamic deploy stage per service
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A `Jenkinsfile` defines a pipeline as code, and there are two styles. A Declarative pipeline uses a structured, opinionated syntax inside a top-level `pipeline` block with fixed sections such as agent, environment, stages, steps, and post. It is easy to read, easy to review, and Jenkins validates its structure before it runs, so a malformed pipeline is rejected early. A Scripted pipeline is written inside a `node` block as a full Groovy program with variables, loops, conditionals, and functions. It is far more flexible but has fewer guardrails, so mistakes surface at runtime and reviewers find it harder to follow.

Groovy is the common foundation. Both styles run on the Jenkins Groovy engine, specifically a sandboxed continuation-passing variant so a pipeline can survive a controller restart. In a Declarative pipeline you still drop into a `script` block of real Groovy when you need genuine logic, while a Scripted pipeline is Groovy from top to bottom. Knowing Groovy matters because you rely on its string interpolation, collections, and closures, and on the steps Jenkins exposes like sh, echo, and error.

My default in a regulated banking environment is Declarative, because audit and review are first-class concerns and the structured form makes the stages, conditions, and failure handling obvious at a glance. I reserve Scripted for genuinely dynamic needs, such as generating a variable number of deploy stages for a list of services discovered at runtime, and even then I push the heavy logic into a Groovy Shared Library so the pipeline file stays small and the complex code lives in one versioned, audited place.

On the banking project the transfer service used a clean Declarative pipeline with Build, Test, and a Deploy stage gated by branch, a post block that always archived artifacts and published test reports, and a failure handler that alerted the channel. The actual deploy logic was a single shared library step, bankDeploy, that every one of our twelve services called, so when we added a vulnerability scan we changed one library file instead of twelve pipelines. The senior point I always add is that I avoid heavy Groovy computation directly in the pipeline because it runs on the controller rather than the agent and can slow the whole instance, and that the CPS sandbox blocks certain methods for security, so library code is the right home for anything non-trivial.
